clinicalPearls: Most fistulae follow the cryptoglandular hypothesis: infection of an anal gland in the intersphincteric plane drains and leaves a chronic epithelialised track between the anal canal and the perianal skin
Typically presents with persistent or intermittent perianal discharge, recurrent abscesses, and a palpable indurated track with an external opening

Goodsall's rule predicts the internal opening: anteriorly placed external openings usually track radially and directly to the anal canal, whereas posterior openings tend to curve to the posterior midline
The Parks classification categorises tracks relative to the sphincter complex as intersphincteric, transsphincteric, suprasphincteric, or extrasphincteric
Complex, multiple, or atypical fistulae should prompt consideration of Crohn's disease, malignancy, tuberculosis, prior radiation, or hidradenitis suppurativa

Treatment depends on how much sphincter the track crosses: fistulotomy (lay-open) suits low simple tracks, while sphincter-preserving options (loose or cutting seton, LIFT, advancement flap, fibrin glue or plug) protect continence in high or complex tracks
Accurate mapping of the track and internal opening with MRI or endoanal ultrasound is central to avoiding recurrence and incontinence
reference.pathophysiology: Most anal fistulae follow the cryptoglandular hypothesis, in which infection of an anal gland at the dentate line lodges in the intersphincteric space and forms an abscess; once this drains, a persistent epithelialised track remains, connecting the internal opening in the anal canal to an external opening on the perianal skin. Chronic inflammation, incomplete drainage, and secondary tracks perpetuate the disease. The relationship of the track to the internal and external sphincters, described by the Parks classification, determines both surgical strategy and the risk to continence. Secondary or atypical fistulae may reflect Crohn's disease, malignancy, or other specific pathology.
additionalInvestigations: Examination under anaesthesia with gentle probing to define the track and internal opening
MRI of the pelvis and anal canal to map complex tracks and secondary extensions
Endoanal ultrasound, with or without hydrogen peroxide enhancement, to delineate the track and sphincters
Assessment for Crohn's disease (ileocolonoscopy) in complex or recurrent disease
Biopsy of atypical or non-healing tracks to exclude malignancy
Anorectal manometry when continence is a concern before dividing any sphincter
redFlags: Multiple, complex, or non-healing fistulae suggesting Crohn's disease or immunosuppression
Induration, irregularity, or a mass raising suspicion of underlying malignancy
Rapidly spreading perianal sepsis or systemic toxicity indicating necrotising infection
A new fistula in a patient with previous pelvic radiotherapy
reference.prognosis: Simple low fistulae treated by fistulotomy generally heal well with low recurrence, but high, complex, or Crohn's-related fistulae are prone to recurrence and to disturbance of continence, often requiring staged sphincter-preserving procedures.
pitfalls: Performing fistulotomy on a high transsphincteric track and causing faecal incontinence
Missing the internal opening or a secondary track, leading to early recurrence
Failing to recognise underlying Crohn's disease before undertaking aggressive surgery
Overlooking malignancy in a chronic, indurated, or atypical fistula
references: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
Keighley & Williams' Surgery of the Anus, Rectum and Colon
management: Drain any associated abscess promptly and place a loose seton to control sepsis before definitive repair
Treat low simple tracks by fistulotomy, which offers reliable healing with low recurrence
Use sphincter-preserving techniques for high or complex tracks, including seton, ligation of the intersphincteric fistula tract, advancement flap, or fibrin glue or plug
Manage Crohn-related fistulae with biologic therapy such as anti-tumour necrosis factor agents alongside seton drainage
Map the track and internal opening preoperatively with examination under anaesthesia and pelvic MRI
Assess sphincter function and continence, including anorectal manometry, before dividing any sphincter
Manage within a colorectal surgical service, particularly for recurrent or complex disease
